Greetings. I have an old laptop from when Windows 7 was new, and want to dual boot with Linux. I have read the sticky and decided that, due to my obsession with security, I should probably choose Debian. Anyway I just have a few questions.

  • Will gaming with Steam still be an issue? I am not interested in running the newest games atm. This laptop can't handle much above Oblivion at max settings.

  • Are there any security issues with dual booting Windows 7 and Debian? I read some in some thread a while back that there was a problem with Amazon spyware in Ubuntu or something. I will see if I can find it.

  • Is it possible, once I build a PC again in the future, to have one external hard drive for Windows, and another for Linux?

  • My old PC got bbq'd (smelled awful). So when I build a new one, I imagine finding Linux compatible parts will be an issue. What can I expect to run into?
Noob here who wants to dual boot. I just have some questions about security and a future PC.

Point by point, from my own experiences:

  • I've never had problems using Steam with Debian, Ubuntu, or Mint. I get the feeling it should work fine on most Debian-based systems.

  • None that I know of. The Amazon spyware wasn't exactly hidden. They were really up-front about how they were going to integrate the desktop search system with Amazon searches.

  • Yes, absolutely. I know I had one friend who actually used a hot-swap drive bay with different OS's on them that didn't have to be set up to dual-boot. As far as any of them knew, they were the only OS on the machine.

  • It's not that much of an issue, if you stick with relatively popular parts. The biggest thing will be making sure drivers work with the hardware you choose. Some manufacturers release Linux drivers for their hardware, some don't. Sometimes those drivers are open-source, sometimes they're not. If the manufacturer-built drivers aren't available or don't work well, you'll have to count on other developers in the Linux community to build them, and that's fine the vast majority of the time. It only gets weird when you're talking about things like a USB dongle to connect to some off-brand Ham radio product that only ever sold 100 units. Nobody has made a driver for that kind of thing, 80% of the time. Oh, also new stuff. Driver developers have to get their hands on the hardware for a while before they can make drivers, so give it a few months before things have settled down.

(For more specific driver advice, expect to have to fiddle with graphics cards, sound cards, touchpad input, and sometimes the stranger network interfaces. None of these should be deal-breakers, though, just a bit rough around the edges.)
Just to add, disabling online search in Ubuntu is insanely easy. It takes all of 10 seconds.

Basically all of that sound fairly on point. I would add that relating to both the laptop and future parts, you are better off with nvidia over AMD/ATI. It may change in the future but for any current hardware you are still better off on team green for discrete video.
Thanks for the detailed reply. I will be honest, I have never built a PC without a hard drive built in it. So this will be new. Probably nothing to it, just something new.

Couple of things I ran into picking up a used Win7 Intel/Intel dual core. Your Linux distro may not use the same clock as Win7. You will wonder what's going wrong, why the Win clock keeps resetting to be off by a few hours, but no minutes. You can make a change in Linux (fairly easy) or tinker with the Win registry. I'm Linux user with low familiarity with Win, so . . . - Second: with a Linux drive and Win7 on separate drives you may run into errors making an image of 7 in the event of disaster. Make the Linux drive removable, try Boot Repair for Linux for plug and chug. Then pull the Linux h.d. to make your image. Viola!

You may find for some uses, printers and scanners for ex, that the Win7 drivers are much easier to use in a plug and play sense. Epson scanner and Bother laser printer. I can use both from Mint/Ubuntu, but the interface is easier with Win.

Steam should work fine. I use it on a Gentoo derivative (Sabayon) and haven't had any issues with it, so Debian should be perfectly fine. The only issue you'll run into is that Debian makes it slightly harder than other distros to install the non-free graphics drivers, which you'll definitely want - see the pages linked here for details.

The spyware in Ubuntu is specific to Unity (the DE in the standard edition) - Ubuntu variants like Kubuntu, Xubuntu, etc. don't have it, and neither does Debian.

External hard drives - this is where it gets interesting. I have no idea if you can install Windows on an external USB hard drive, though you can certainly try and see what happens. I once managed to run WinXP off a USB drive, but there have probably been too many changes since then to rely on that. (If you use (e)SATA to connect the drive it should work fine though.)

Linux should run off an external drive without any problems at all. That said, you have an easier time if you just install both (on separate partitions) on the internal drive. You can always swap it out for a larger one, and it'll be significantly faster than a USB one.

Hardware compatibility - the parts you want check are motherboard, graphics card, wifi (less relevant for a desktop) and printer.

For the motherboard you just need to google the model no. (e.g. "ga-990fxa-ud3 linux") and see if there are any known issues with it. (As an aside, I do not recommend that motherboard - USB3 on it is a bit unreliable.)

Graphics card - either use Intel's integrated graphics (with open source driver) or Nvidia (with proprietary driver - nouveau is much slower). As much as I like AMD, you'll find their drivers to be quite frustrating, and Linux support for Steam games is often Nvidia-only.

Wifi, printer - just check that a driver exists, or that you can use one of the generic drivers.

Also, if you're obsessed with security, take a look at AppArmor - it takes a little tinkering, but it provides more fine-grained control than the traditional approach.
Linux Mint Debian Edition 2. x64 Mate. Your laptop will handle more than it did in Windows, most likely. It really does depend on video drivers.
